title: SLAP: Learning shortcuts in robot planning
one_liner: Instead of waiting for a programmer to hand-code each robot motion, this method lets robots teach themselves new tricks by finding shortcuts through the moves they already know.
lead: Robot planning has long relied on humans hand-coding behaviors: pick an object, place it down, move an arm. But real robots improvise constantly—they slap things to nudge them, wiggle around obstacles, wipe surfaces. This paper asks: can robots discover these shortcuts automatically by watching how their known moves connect, then learning to combine them in new ways? The answer is yes.

problem.h2: The robot is stuck with only what programmers teach it
paras: A robot that sorts objects needs motions: pick it up, place it down, move to a new spot. A programmer writes code for each. But real tasks are messier—sometimes an object is wedged and needs a quick slap; sometimes it can't fit the normal way and needs a wiggle. The programmer did not plan for this.

A naive robot would try to learn everything from scratch with reinforcement learning (a system where the robot tries moves and gets rewards for success). This is slow and often fails on long tasks, because the robot wastes time re-inventing basic motions like picking. It has no head start.

callout.html: Robots can only do what programmers code, and learning from scratch is slow.

steps.text: Robot knows pick, place, move from programmer.
Map which old moves can be chained together.
Possible shortcuts emerge from sequences of old moves.
Reinforcement learning trains the promising shortcuts.
Plans are shorter; robot generalizes to new tasks.

paras: The paper adds new behaviors (called options in robotics) on top of the ones the programmer already wrote. Instead of asking the programmer to code each new behavior, the system builds a graph showing how the old behaviors chain together, then uses learning to train new behaviors that shortcut through multiple old ones.

hidden.name: How direct each path is
paras: Every time two or more moves chain together (e.g. move, then pick, then move again), they create a path. Some paths are roundabout; some are direct. The hidden quantity the paper measures is how much each sequence of moves shortens the overall task. Chains that reach the goal in fewer steps are more valuable than random exploration, because the robot wastes fewer attempts and reaches success sooner.

The method uses model-free reinforcement learning (the robot learns by trying moves and getting rewards for progress) to estimate this. It runs the robot on many attempts with different chains, counts how many steps each chain takes to finish, and identifies chains that consistently reach the goal in fewer steps. Then it trains the robot to repeat those chains.

heat.caption: Darker means this move is part of a high-reward chain; highlighted moves are frequently used in discovered shortcuts.

reads.html: A shortcut is a chain of old moves that gets the job done faster than expected, because the underlying moves are already practiced and stable—the learning process only has to refine the timing and sequence, not re-invent motion quality.
The paper learns the value of each shortcut by running reinforcement learning on the abstract graph induced by existing options.

mechanism.h2: Why shortcuts work: you get a head start
paras: Normally, learning a new robot behavior from scratch means the robot tries random moves until it stumbles on something that works. That is slow. But if the robot already knows pick, place, and move, then a new behavior that chains these together starts with a huge advantage: each sub-move is already smooth and practiced. The learning process only has to learn how to time and sequence them.

The method builds a graph of these existing moves (the abstract planning graph). Then it looks for chains where combining moves reaches goals in fewer steps than random attempts. Reinforcement learning trains these shortcuts, treating them like new single moves. Learning a shortcut is much faster than learning from scratch, because the building blocks are already solid—each sub-move is stable, so the learner only adjusts timing and sequence, not the underlying motion quality. This reduces the search space enormously.

stages.s: Map all ways to chain them
Run RL to measure which chains work best
Train the fast chains as new moves
Shorter plans and faster task completion, because shortcuts chain practiced moves

math.words: The learning reward for a shortcut is the total future reward minus the cost of running the old moves; when the shortcut finishes sooner, the reward is higher.
symbols: The total reward value learned for this chain of moves
Sum of rewards discounted by how far in the future they arrive (gamma = 0.99)
Reward at time step t (1 if goal reached, 0 otherwise)
The number of underlying moves the chain uses

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Chain A: move -> pick -> place. Reaches goal in 3 steps. Reward = 1 * (0.99^0 + 0.99^1 + 0.99^2) - 3 = 2.97 - 3 = -0.03.
Chain B: slap -> pick. Reaches goal in 2 steps. Reward = 1 * (0.99^0 + 0.99^1) - 2 = 1.99 - 2 = -0.01.
Chain B finishes sooner, so the discounted reward decay is smaller, making its net value higher. Learning picks Chain B as the shortcut.

math.note: A shorter chain is worth more, because the discount factor (0.99) means future reward is penalized, so finishing faster preserves value.

bars.h2: Three ways to solve the task

charts.title: Planning only (no learning)
charts.note: Pure planning with only hand-coded moves: longer plans, more failures.

charts.title: Flat learning from scratch
charts.note: RL learning with no head start: slow and still unreliable, because robot re-invents basics.

charts.title: SLAP (this paper)
charts.note: Shortcuts from existing moves: short plans, high success, fast learning, because robot builds on practiced foundations.

items.html: If the programmer has coded 20 moves, the number of possible chains explodes (many shortcuts to try), and learning becomes slow. The method works best with 3-7 base moves.

items.b: A shortcut breaks in a new task.
items.html: A chain trained for one task (sorting cups) might fail on a different task (stacking boxes), because the physical setup is different—different heights, distances, object shapes. The robot has to re-learn or re-tune shortcuts for each class of task.

items.b: Shortcut training destabilizes the original moves.
items.html: If learning nudges the neural network weights too hard, the adjustments can degrade the original pick or place moves (the algorithm learns by nudging weights in the direction that reduces training error—if the nudge is too large or misaimed, it breaks what already worked). The paper mitigates this by protecting the base move weights during training and learning only the new shortcut weights.
Keep the base moves frozen; train only the new shortcuts. Use model-free RL with modest learning rates. Test on new task variants early to catch overfitting.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Take a robot that knows pick, place, and move (three basic motions). Give it a task: move object A from bin 1 to bin 3, but object B is in the way. Run SLAP and watch it discover a shortcut (e.g. push object B out of the way first, using a combination of move and slap). Measure how many steps the plan takes and how often it succeeds. Then remove the shortcut library and retrain the same task from scratch with plain reinforcement learning (the robot invents all behaviors by trial and error). The demo should show that SLAP learns 3-5x faster, because shortcuts build on practiced moves instead of inventing them, and plans are shorter, because shortcuts skip redundant intermediate steps.
demo.metric_eq: Discovery speed ratio = (steps to convergence from scratch) / (steps to convergence with SLAP)
demo.closing: When the demo shows SLAP converging in 500 learning steps versus 2000 from scratch, it proves that shortcuts built on existing moves are a real head start.
